La información de la nariz, en cambio, llega casi sin escalas a la amígdala, que gestiona el miedo y la emoción, así que un olor puede reactivar un recuerdo cargado de sentimiento antes incluso de que lo reconozcas conscientemente.
detail.en: Sight, hearing and touch all pass through the thalamus first before getting processed. Information from the nose, by contrast, arrives almost without a layover at the amygdala, which handles fear and emotion, so a smell can reactivate an emotionally loaded memory before you've even consciously recognized it.

source: Psychology Today — How the Sense of Smell Triggers Old and Long-Forgotten Memories
_evidence: Smell is the only sense that transmits sensory information directly to the amygdala, the brain region that processes fear and arousal.

question.es: Cuando tienes la nariz taponada, ¿por qué de repente la comida no sabe casi a nada?
question.en: When your nose is stuffed up, why does food suddenly barely taste like anything?

answer.es: Porque la mayor parte de lo que llamas "sabor" en realidad lo capta la nariz, no la lengua.
answer.en: Because most of what you call "taste" is actually picked up by the nose, not the tongue.

detail.es: Mientras masticas, las moléculas de aroma suben por dentro, desde la garganta hasta la nariz, y activan cientos de receptores olfativos, un proceso llamado olfacción retronasal. La lengua solo distingue lo básico, dulce, salado, amargo; todo el resto del sabor depende de ese circuito interno, y un resfriado lo bloquea sin tocar las papilas para nada.
detail.en: While you chew, aroma molecules travel up internally, from the throat to the nose, and activate hundreds of smell receptors, a process called retronasal olfaction. The tongue only tells basic sweet, salty, bitter apart; the rest of flavor depends on that internal circuit, and a cold blocks it without touching the taste buds at all.

source: Ask A Biologist, Arizona State University — Does Smell Affect Taste?
_evidence: It is the activation of these receptors that primarily affects the flavor of food. This is called retronasal olfaction... Think about when you have a stuffed-up nose during a head cold – food doesn't quite taste the same, right?

question.es: ¿Cómo recibe oxígeno la córnea de tu ojo si no tiene ni un solo vaso sanguíneo dentro?
question.en: How does your cornea get oxygen if it doesn't have a single blood vessel inside it?

answer.es: Lo toma directamente del aire: se disuelve en la lágrima y de ahí pasa a las células.
answer.en: It takes it straight from the air: it dissolves into the tear film and passes into the cells from there.

detail.es: Si la córnea tuviera venas, como casi cualquier otro tejido, no serías capaz de ver a través de ella con nitidez. En vez de eso, respira literalmente del aire: el oxígeno se disuelve en la fina capa de lágrima que la cubre y difunde hacia el tejido, así que cerrar los ojos mucho tiempo, como al dormir, le corta buena parte de ese suministro.
detail.en: If the cornea had veins, like almost every other tissue, you wouldn't be able to see clearly through it. Instead, it literally breathes from the air: oxygen dissolves into the thin tear layer covering it and diffuses into the tissue, so keeping your eyes closed for a long stretch, like during sleep, cuts off a good part of that supply.

source: Cleveland Clinic — Cornea
_evidence: Tear fluid provides lubrication for your eye surface and helps the epithelium absorb oxygen from the air.

question.es: ¿Por qué al rato de entrar en tu propia casa dejas de notar cómo huele, aunque un visitante sí lo note?
question.en: Why do you stop noticing how your own house smells shortly after walking in, even though a visitor does?

answer.es: Porque el cerebro apaga un olor concreto en cuanto decide que ya es familiar y no supone ningún peligro.
answer.en: Because the brain switches off one specific smell as soon as it decides it's familiar and poses no danger.

detail.es: Es un reflejo antiguo de supervivencia: si un olor sigue presente sin cambiar y no ha resultado ser una amenaza, el cerebro deja de gastar atención en procesarlo para quedar libre ante señales nuevas. Es un apagado muy específico del olor en cuestión, así que la misma nariz insensible al ambiente de casa detecta al instante un perfume nuevo.
detail.en: It's an ancient survival reflex: if a smell stays present without changing and hasn't turned out to be a threat, the brain stops spending attention processing it so it stays free for new signals. The shutdown is very specific to that one smell, so the same nose that's numb to the house's own air instantly picks up on a new perfume.

source: Wikipedia — Olfactory fatigue
_evidence: the temporary, normal inability to distinguish a particular odor after a prolonged exposure to that airborne compound.

question.es: Si bostezar no sirve para tomar más oxígeno, como se creía, ¿para qué sirve realmente?
question.en: If yawning isn't about taking in more oxygen, like people used to think, what's it actually for?

answer.es: Para refrigerar el cerebro: el aire que entra de golpe le baja la temperatura por dentro.
answer.en: To cool the brain down: the sudden rush of incoming air lowers its internal temperature.

detail.es: Durante décadas se dio por hecho que bostezar compensaba una falta de oxígeno en sangre, pero ningún estudio ha logrado probar esa relación. La investigación de Gallup muestra en cambio que la gente bosteza más quieta y con más frecuencia en invierno que en pleno verano, justo lo que cabría esperar si su función real fuera mantener el cerebro dentro de una temperatura óptima.
detail.en: For decades it was assumed yawning made up for low blood oxygen, but no study has ever managed to prove that link. Gallup's research instead shows people yawn more often in winter than in the height of summer, exactly what you'd expect if its real job is keeping the brain within an optimal temperature window.

source: ScienceDaily — Do we yawn to cool the brain?
_evidence: Common belief is that yawning helps to increase the oxygen supply. However, previous research has failed to show an association between yawning and blood oxygen levels... yawning cools the brain.

question.es: ¿Puedes oler humo o goma quemada con total claridad sin que haya nada quemándose cerca?
question.en: Can you smell smoke or burning rubber with total clarity when nothing nearby is actually burning?

answer.es: Sí: se llama fantosmia, una alucinación olfativa que el cerebro genera sin ningún estímulo real.
answer.en: Yes: it's called phantosmia, an olfactory hallucination the brain generates with no real stimulus at all.

detail.es: Quien la sufre percibe olores, casi siempre desagradables como humo, goma quemada o metal, que no vienen de ningún sitio exterior. Puede deberse a algo tan simple como una sinusitis o disparase por migrañas, y en la mayoría de los casos desaparece por sí sola sin dejar ninguna secuela.
detail.en: People who experience it perceive smells, almost always unpleasant ones like smoke, burning rubber or metal, that come from nowhere in the outside world. It can stem from something as simple as sinusitis or get triggered by migraines, and in most cases it fades away on its own without leaving any lasting effect.

source: Cleveland Clinic — Phantosmia (Olfactory Hallucinations)
_evidence: a condition that causes you to detect smells that aren't actually present in your environment (phantom smells)

question.es: ¿Por qué tantos recién nacidos tienen los ojos azul grisáceo y luego les cambian de color?
question.en: Why are so many newborns born with grayish-blue eyes that later change color?

answer.es: Porque dentro del útero no hay luz, y sin luz el iris todavía no ha empezado a producir pigmento.
answer.en: Because there's no light inside the womb, and without light the iris hasn't started producing pigment yet.

detail.es: Las células que fabrican melanina en el iris, los melanocitos, se activan con la exposición a la luz una vez el bebé nace. Cuanta más luz reciben los ojos en los primeros meses, más pigmento generan esas células, así que el color puede seguir cambiando hasta los nueve meses o el año de vida, y no se fija del todo hasta los tres años.
detail.en: The melanin-producing cells in the iris, melanocytes, switch on with light exposure once the baby is born. The more light the eyes take in during the first months, the more pigment those cells generate, so the color can keep shifting until nine months or a year old, and doesn't fully settle until age three.

source: Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials — When Do Babies' Eyes Change Color?
_evidence: Many babies have lighter, blue-gray eyes due to less pigment in their irises... a baby's eyes — specifically cells in the iris called melanocytes — are exposed to light, and that produces pigment, or color.
